chunks: Source vs sink termination and matching. The question: What is the difference and tradeoffs of source vs sink termination/matching?
A signal on a fast wire is a wave, and a wave bounces back from any end that doesn't absorb it. The sending end is the source and the receiving end is the sink.
"Matching" an end means giving it a resistance equal to the wire's own impedance, so it soaks up the wave instead of bouncing it. You can match the source, the sink, or both.
Each choice absorbs the bounce at a different place.
Picture throwing a ball down a long corridor. A catcher with a glove at the far end (sink matching) catches it on arrival, so nothing bounces.
With no catcher, the ball hits the far wall and returns, and the thrower catches it (source matching). Every catcher takes energy, though.
In a circuit the matching resistors form a divider, so matching both ends costs half the voltage.
The two schemes differ in time and place of absorption.
Source termination absorbs after a round trip (the sink sees full swing at t d , but a mid-line receiver sees half swing until the reflection passes).
Sink termination absorbs at the first arrival, so there is nothing to come back.
Characteristic impedance ( Z 0 ): the resistance a wire "looks like" to a wave traveling along it ("Characteristic impedance explained").
Reflection: the part of a wave that bounces back from a mismatched end ("Reflections and why they matter").
Source resistance: the driver's own output resistance plus any resistor added in series with it. Echo: a bounced wave that arrives again later, distorting the signal.
Divider: two resistances in a row that split a voltage between them.
Use a 3. 3 volts source with 50 ohms of source resistance and a 50 ohms wire. If the far end is open, the wave leaves at 1. 65 volts, doubles to 3.
3 volts at the receiver, and the bounce is absorbed at the source. Now add a 50 ohms resistor to ground at the receiver.
The wave is absorbed on arrival, nothing bounces, and the receiver sees 3. 3 times 50 over (50 plus 50) equals 1. 65 volts.
That is double matching: very clean, but only half the voltage. That is the whole idea.

"Source termination matches the driver so reflections coming back are absorbed at the near end: cheap, no DC power, but the full level only appears after a round trip, so it suits one receiver at the end.
Sink termination matches the receiver so the wave is absorbed on arrival: clean edges for every receiver, tolerant of driver impedance, but costs DC power and swing.
Doing both is double termination, standard in RF and on-die termination links, very forgiving, but the amplitude is only half the source voltage."
